entries.note: Two lanes independently taught the launcher to pass --session-id: the identity (spec 095) minted one, the host's conversation (spec 096) minted another, and merged as-is a pane would have carried both with different UUIDs. The reconciliation is that the conversation IS the identity, and this function is the single place that decides which id that is, for any CLI whose recipe declares a conversation (spec 114). Order matters and is deliberate: the person's own flags first (the recipe's parser), because launch.mjs reports the decided id back to the host over /api/agent-conversation and the record must follow what actually launched rather than what the host intended — a contradiction between the two is resolved in the person's favour, not refused; then a bound session (bind.mjs's --session, or codex's handoff); then the host's RENGINE_AGENT_CONVERSATION for an ordinary pane — kept only when the recipe can start it or the pane resumes it, since a CLI with no start spelling (kimi, codex) cannot be told which conversation to START; then a mint. -c/--continue, a search-term --resume, a bare selector and --fork-session return id null with source 'unknown', which makes plan.conversation null and tells the host to claim nothing.

entries.note: Each launch creates a private unique configuration directory so concurrent agents cannot overwrite one another's overlays. User files are never rewritten. The overlay an agent gets is its recipe's mcp.kind (registry.mjs, spec 114), dispatched by kind rather than by CLI name: 'flag' is the generic --mcp-config channel (claude, which also gets the per-launch settings and the IDE decision when the recipe says so), 'config-args' is codex's -c dotted overrides (which also carry the SessionStart hook and its same-launch trusted_hash — see codex-hooks-trust-themselves), 'env-inline' is OpenCode's config JSON in an environment variable, 'env-defaults' is Gemini's lowest-precedence defaults file (managed policy stays authoritative), and 'project-file' is the deliberate exception to 'never rewritten' (spec 127): kimi publishes no flag, env or overlay channel at all, only a project-level .kimi-code/mcp.json, so the launch writes THAT file — at the pane's repository root, preserving every foreign entry and reclaiming only rEngine's rengine_ namespace. Malformed input or a name collision in a preserved file fails visibly. Codex requires the injected MCP server to initialize; no permission-bypass flags are supplied. conversationArgs names the conversation exactly once for an identity rEngine decided, and adds nothing to a launch whose own args already name a session, because the identity IS that session id.

entries.note: kimi publishes exactly one per-project MCP channel: .kimi-code/mcp.json at the repository root — no --mcp-config flag, no environment override, and a user-level file rEngine refuses to touch (global mutable state; a KIMI_CODE_HOME redirect would move the person's login and sessions). So unlike every other named CLI, the wiring is a write into the project itself, and the rules mirror that: every entry outside the rengine_ namespace is the project's and is preserved verbatim, invalid JSON is refused with the file untouched, and the namespace is reclaimed whole because a stale key in it points at a per-launch context that no longer exists. The root is found by walking to the nearest .git from the pane's cwd — kimi resolves project level the same way — falling back to the cwd. The file is shared and last-writer-wins across panes, which is why mcp.mjs resolves its context from the pane's own environment before this file's argv (spec 127 decision 5).

entries.note: Codex runs a non-managed hook only when hooks.state."<key>".trusted_hash equals the sha256 of its normalized definition; anything else waits for a manual /hooks review, and every launch's unique context path would make every pane a new review prompt. So the launch trusts exactly what it composed: the key is codex's synthetic session-flags layer path (stable across launches), the hash covers this launch's command, and both ride the same -c layer as the hook itself — per-key merge means the person's own hooks keep their gate and ~/.codex is never written. --dangerously-bypass-hook-trust was rejected: it would also waive review for untrusted PROJECT-layer hooks, which is the attack the gate exists for. The formula was reverse-engineered from codex-rs (hook_hash → version_for_toml) and verified byte-exact against codex 0.153.4's own hooks/list app-server method before any TUI ran; the naive dot-split -c parser is why the state entry is one TOML table under hooks.state rather than a dotted key. If a codex upgrade changes the normalization (e.g. a new default field), the hash silently stops matching and the hook waits for review — the agent-registry test pins the composition, and re-verification is the hooks/list call in docs/evidence/codex-sessionstart-hook-2026-09-11.md.
